strengths: The Attention Matching objective is well-motivated and cleanly derived: the observation that attention over concatenated blocks decomposes into a mass-weighted mixture (Eq. 5, Appendix A.2) gives a principled reason to match both local attention output and attention mass, and clearly explains why token-eviction baselines systematically underestimate the compacted block's contribution.

The per-token scalar bias β is a simple but effective idea, with a crisp argument for its necessity (exact mass matching is impossible with t < T), and it is supported in standard attention kernels with negligible overhead.

The decomposition into key selection, β fitting (NNLS), and value fitting (least squares) with closed-form steps is elegant and avoids gradient descent at compaction time; the family of variants (OMP, OMP-fast, HighestAttnKeys) traces a genuine speed-quality frontier.

Comprehensive and careful experimental work: three models across two model families plus a hybrid sliding-window model, multiple strong baselines including Cartridges, KVzip, H2O+, SnapKV, PyramidKV, and multiple summarization prompts, with a detailed time breakdown (Table 1) and leave-one-out ablations (Figure 4).

Honest, specific limitations discussion: Cartridges wins at 100× on some benchmarks, OMP is slow in the unoptimized variant, compaction still takes several minutes; the paper also carefully documents where reconstruction loss is and is not a valid proxy (Appendix F.2).

Notable extensions add value: combining summarization with AM for ~200× compaction (Table 2), precomputed nonuniform head budgets grounded in input-invariant sensitivity curves, and a preliminary online-compaction AIME result showing reasoning state survives repeated mid-trajectory compaction.
Reproducibility is strong: algorithms are given in full, prompts and hyperparameters are enumerated, solvers and numerics choices are documented, and compute budgets for baselines are reported.
weaknesses: Benchmark coverage is narrow. Only QuALITY (50 contexts, 5–7k tokens) and LongHealth (only 4 contexts, 400 questions) are used. LongHealth results rest on just 4 evaluation contexts, and there are no results on broader long-context suites (e.g., RULER, LongBench, needle-based retrieval), so generality of the accuracy claims is only weakly supported.

Cartridges, the closest and most important competitor, is evaluated on only one model and a 20-article subset whose original-cache accuracy (75.0%) differs from the full set (72.1%), making the head-to-head comparison against the headline competitor somewhat fragile, and Cartridges may benefit from an easier subset.

'Fast' is relative: query generation (self-study + repeat-prefill) dominates runtime and still requires several minutes per context, and compaction itself requires a full prefill; the practical advantage over training-free baselines like KVzip (which sometimes matches AM, attributed to budget-allocation differences) is narrower than the abstract framing suggests.

The method is justified as an approximation at the single-layer level; there is no analysis of how per-layer approximation errors compound across sequentially compacted layers, and the on-policy query correction is a heuristic patch rather than a principled treatment.

Evaluation protocol asymmetries: KV-based chunked compaction is applied to all baselines except Cartridges on LongHealth, and the LongHealth context length (60k, 5 patients) is reduced relative to the original Cartridges setting (10 patients), partly justified by model brittleness but still complicating direct comparison.
Claims about scaling to much larger models (e.g., Qwen3-235B) are extrapolation from KV-cache size arguments rather than experiments; the largest model tested is 12B.

The paper does not explicitly commit to releasing code; given the many implementation subtleties (β stabilization rules, solver choices, chunking details), reproduction without code would be difficult despite the detailed appendix.

strengths: The Attention Matching objective is well motivated and technically clean: the decomposition of attention over concatenated blocks into locally normalized outputs weighted by attention mass (Appendix A.2) gives a principled reason to match both outputs and mass, and explains why per-token biases are necessary (e.g., q=0 requiring T vs t mass matching).

The method avoids gradient descent at compaction time entirely: OMP for key selection, NNLS for mass fitting, and least squares for value fitting are efficient closed-form subroutines, and the resulting speed/quality trade-off (Figure 1, Table 1) is a genuine and useful contribution to the Pareto frontier relative to both token-eviction baselines and the much slower Cartridges.

Evaluation is reasonably broad: three model families (Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma3-12B), two long-context benchmarks, six baselines with carefully reconstructed question-agnostic configurations (Table 4), an ablation of every major component (Figure 4), timing breakdowns, and an interesting extension combining compaction with summarization (Table 2) and online mid-trajectory compaction (Appendix F.3).

The nonuniform head-budget component is supported by a useful empirical observation (head sensitivity curves are largely input-invariant and transfer across datasets), and the paper is honest that KVzip's implicit global allocation sometimes beats their precomputed budgets.

The paper treats limitations candidly (e.g., Cartridges outperforming at 100x on LongHealth, several minutes still required for OMP variants, LongHealth brittleness attributed to the base model beyond ~100k tokens), which is appropriate scientific practice.
weaknesses: The evaluation is confined to two multiple-choice QA benchmarks (QuALITY, LongHealth). Both measure comprehension-style extraction; there is no evidence on generation-heavy, retrieval, code, or agentic tasks where compaction quality claims would matter most, so the generality of the central claim ('little quality loss') is only partially supported.

Model scale is modest (4B-12B). The claim that efficiency results will 'scale without much additional cost' to larger models (Section 4.3) is an extrapolation supported only by a KV-cache size argument, not by measurement.

The headline comparison with Cartridges is narrow: it is run on only one model (Qwen3-4B), on only 20 of 50 QuALITY contexts for the accuracy sweep, and with default (possibly suboptimal) Cartridges hyperparameters, as the authors themselves acknowledge. Given that Cartridges is the primary framing target, this comparison is thinner than ideal.

Wall-clock timing comparisons conflate method-independent costs: query generation dominates runtime and varies with the chosen query-sampling strategy, and all timing is on a single GPU with a specific chunk size; the 'orders of magnitude faster' claim is hardware- and configuration-dependent and is not decomposed in a way that allows clean cross-paper verification.

The evaluation sizes are small for the variance levels typical of these benchmarks: 894 questions on QuALITY (fewer for the Cartridges comparison), 4 LongHealth contexts of 100 questions each. No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals on accuracy are reported in the main results.

The approach requires per-token scalar attention bias support in the serving stack; while common kernels are cited as supporting this, the paper does not measure the runtime/memory overhead of the bias path in a real inference engine, and the (2t+d)/t overhead factor is only argued qualitatively.

No code release or artifact link is provided despite extensive implementation detail (solver choices, hyperparameters like k=4, tau=2, bias clamping thresholds); given the many small engineering choices that affect results, reproducibility without code is questionable.

There is noticeable overlap with KVzip, which also performs query-agnostic cache reconstruction; the paper's differentiation (attention output + mass matching with biases vs. reconstruction loss) is stated but the empirical comparison of the two objectives in isolation is limited to the ablation setting rather than a direct head-to-head of the objectives themselves.

strengths: Well-motivated and cleanly formulated objective: the paper decomposes context compaction into matching (i) locally normalized attention outputs and (ii) attention mass, and rigorously justifies why this preserves behavior under concatenation with arbitrary future tokens via the mixture identity (Appendix A.2, Eq. 5). The per-token scalar bias β is a natural and well-argued contribution that fixes the systematic mass underestimation of pure token dropping.

Strong algorithmic contribution: the observation that the objective admits closed-form solutions (NNLS for β, least squares for Cv, OMP for key selection) avoids gradient descent entirely at compaction time, yielding a family of methods tracing the speed-quality Pareto frontier. The OMP formulation for sparse mass matching over key columns is elegant.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 3 model families (Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-3-12B), two long-context benchmarks, full compaction-ratio sweeps, strong baselines (Cartridges, KVzip, H2O+, SnapKV, PyramidKV, multiple summarization prompts), timing breakdowns (Table 1), leave-one-out ablations (Figure 4), query-sampling ablations (Figure 5), head-budget analysis, and a comparison of reconstruction loss vs. downstream accuracy (F.2) that is unusually honest about when loss is/isn't a good proxy.

Practical significance is high: matching or beating Cartridges quality at 50x compaction while being ~2 orders of magnitude faster addresses a real deployment bottleneck (agentic/tool-heavy contexts, prefix caching). The extension showing 200x compaction by applying AM on top of summarization, and the online mid-trajectory compaction proof-of-concept on AIME (F.3), broaden applicability.

Reproducibility is above average: detailed algorithmic appendix (OMP with periodic refit, NNLS solver with projected gradient descent, solver comparisons, β stabilization rules, chunked compaction details, exact self-study prompts, baseline configurations in Table 4).

Honest limitations discussion: acknowledges Cartridges wins at 100x, that unoptimized variants take minutes, that KVzip's non-uniform budget sometimes wins, and that gradient-based methods search a wider space at extreme ratios.
weaknesses: Benchmark breadth is narrow: evaluation is limited to two multiple-choice QA benchmarks (QuALITY, LongHealth). Standard long-context suites (RULER, LongBench variants, NIAH-style retrieval, code, or free-form generation tasks) are absent, so the generality of the compaction primitive beyond MCQA-style information extraction is not established. The F.2 analysis itself shows summarization can preserve QA accuracy despite poor reconstruction, highlighting that MCQA accuracy may under-measure behavioral preservation in other task types.

Small evaluation sets raise statistical concerns: LongHealth uses only 4 contexts (400 questions); QuALITY uses 50 articles; Cartridges is evaluated on only a 20-context subset and only on Qwen3-4B. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for the headline accuracy comparisons, and differences between AM-OMP, KVzip, and Cartridges in Figure 3 are sometimes small.

Wall-clock comparisons deserve more careful accounting: query generation (prefill + self-study generation, ~150s on LongHealth) dominates the method's runtime and requires extra forward passes; baselines like KVzip also perform a reconstruction pass, but the fairness of the timing comparisons and the potential for the same query-generation machinery to boost token-eviction baselines (e.g., 'HighestAttnKeys' differs from KVzip largely by value/bias refitting) are only partially disentangled in the ablations.

The method is heuristic in its query-distribution assumption: matching attention on reference queries provides no guarantee for out-of-distribution future queries, and the distribution-shift mitigation ('on-policy' sequential layer compaction) is only described as yielding 'slight but consistent improvements' without error analysis of when the proxy distribution fails.

The nonuniform head-budget procedure has several hyperparameters (η, step size, reference ratio r0=0.05, sensitivity-curve sample size of 10 articles) whose sensitivity is not studied; the 'stability across contexts' claim is supported for two models but the greedy swap algorithm's robustness at other operating points is unclear.

Some system-level claims are lightly supported: the assertion that biases add 'negligible-to-zero' runtime and are supported in common attention kernels is not benchmarked in the paper, and nonuniform caches relying on varlen packing are discussed (footnote 3) but not measured end-to-end for actual serving throughput/memory savings.

DuoAttention is implemented but omitted from the main figure after poor performance; given it is a natural nonuniform-comparison point for Llama-3.1-8B, more detail on the failure mode would strengthen the evaluation.

strengths: The core formulation is clean and well-motivated: the paper derives a mixture decomposition of attention over concatenated blocks (Appendix A.2, Eq. 5) showing that matching (i) locally normalized attention output and (ii) attention mass is a sufficient condition for compaction to be compatible with arbitrary future tokens. This gives the method a principled foundation rather than being pure engineering, and the derivation of why per-token scalar biases are necessary (e.g., q=0 requires matching T vs t; subset selection systematically underestimates mass) is convincing.

The decomposition of the joint optimization into (Ck, β, Cv) with closed-form subroutines (NNLS for β, OLS for Cv) is elegant and practically important, allowing compaction without gradient descent — which is the key enabler of the orders-of-magnitude speedup over Cartridges.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough: five benchmarks (QuALITY, LongHealth, QASPER, LongBench v2, RULER) spanning multiple-choice QA, free-form generative QA, and retrieval-intensive tasks; three model families including a sliding-window model (Gemma-3); comparisons against strong recent baselines (KVzip, SnapKV, PyramidKV, KVMerger, H2O) and Cartridges; plus efficiency profiling (Table 3) and leave-one-out ablations (Figure 5) showing every component contributes.

The paper is honest and precise about limitations: it acknowledges that Cartridges outperforms AM at extreme 100× compaction on some benchmarks, explains why (gradient methods search a richer space), notes that unoptimized OMP variants take minutes, and identifies MLA incompatibility. The limitations discussion is candid rather than defensive.

Notable extensions add value beyond the main method: the model-specific nonuniform head budgets (with evidence that head sensitivity rankings are input-invariant and transfer across datasets), chunked compaction with careful RoPE/positional handling, the summarization+AM composition (Table 4), and the online mid-trajectory compaction proof-of-concept on AIME (Table 9) which suggests a genuinely interesting future direction for long-horizon reasoning.

Baseline treatment is careful and fair: question-aware methods are converted to question-agnostic protocols, GQA query aggregation is handled correctly, chat-template tokens are fixed consistently, and the Cartridges compute is replicated at the same order of magnitude of self-study tokens.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'preserving model behavior for any future queries' rests on matching attention only over reference queries whose distribution is generated by the model itself (self-study/repeat-prefill). The paper shows self-study beats random vectors, but there is no direct test of robustness when actual downstream queries differ substantially in distribution from the reference queries (e.g., adversarial or out-of-distribution query styles). The observed LongBench v2/QASPER generalization partially mitigates this, but the distribution-shift risk is not quantified.

The Cartridges comparison is the headline framing (Figure 1) yet is evaluated on only one model and a fixed 20-context subset of QuALITY, using default repository settings that the authors themselves note are unoptimized. While the ~5 GPU-hours/context cost is real, the claim of 'exceeding Cartridges while being 2 orders of magnitude faster' would be more convincing with a Cartridges variant with improved training efficiency.

Some evaluation protocols are slightly unusual and could bias toward the proposed method: LongBench v2 restricts to a 47-context subset selected via full-context-correct/no-context-incorrect filtering (though all methods are re-run on it), and LongHealth uses only 4 contexts. Statistical power on the latter is limited despite 100 questions per context.

The method family is heavily engineered with many interacting design choices (OMP variants k/τ, β stabilization bounds, RMS vs mean/max aggregation, KV- vs text-based chunking, on-policy sequential layer compaction, precomputed head budgets). The ablations address the main components, but the large hyperparameter surface raises questions about which configuration is actually being recommended for practitioners and about potential overfitting of design choices to the evaluated benchmarks.

Key selection is restricted to a subset of original keys, which is acknowledged as a fundamental expressiveness limitation relative to Cartridges; the most interesting direction (directly optimizing compact keys without gradient descent) is deferred to future work, leaving the method somewhat incremental in terms of representation power.

No explicit code release statement appears in the manuscript. Given the number of implementation details that matter (NNLS solver choices, β stabilization, chunking, RoPE phase alignment), reproducibility would be substantially strengthened by a released implementation, and its absence is a concern.

strengths: The core formulation is well motivated and technically clean: the decomposition of attention over concatenated blocks into locally normalized outputs weighted by unnormalized attention mass (Appendix A.2, Eq. 5) provides a principled justification for jointly matching attention outputs (Eq. 1) and attention mass (Eq. 2), and clearly explains why per-token biases β are necessary (Mass(q; Ck) ≤ Mass(q; K) for subset selection).

The claim that the objective decomposes into efficient subroutines is genuinely delivered: β via NNLS, Cv via closed-form least squares, and Ck via either an RMS-aggregated highest-attention heuristic or OMP with NNLS refitting (Algorithm 1), avoiding gradient descent at compaction time. The mixture-identity argument makes the case that this avoids the systematic underestimation of the compacted block's contribution that plagues plain eviction methods.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this area: three model families (Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-3-12B including a sliding-window architecture), five benchmarks (QuALITY, LongHealth, QASPER, LongBench v2, RULER), multiple strong baselines (Cartridges, KVzip, SnapKV, PyramidKV, H2O+, KVMerger, summarization), component ablations (Figure 5), timing breakdowns (Table 3), and head-budget analysis (Figures 3, 7–9).

Baseline treatment is careful and fair: question-aware methods (SnapKV, PyramidKV) are made question-agnostic via mock questions, H2O is adapted to the one-shot setting, GQA query aggregation is handled explicitly, and the design choices of every baseline are documented (Table 6).

The paper is honest about limitations: Cartridges wins at extreme (100×) ratios on some benchmarks, the strongest OMP variants take several minutes, β can degenerate (with mitigation described), and the online-compaction results are presented as a proof of concept rather than a headline claim.

The online/mid-trajectory compaction experiment (Table 9, AIME) is a compelling demonstration that the compaction primitive composes repeatedly without destroying reasoning state, going beyond the standard one-shot QA evaluation.
weaknesses: The central search problem—selecting Ck—does not actually admit a closed-form solution; the method restricts Ck to a subset of original keys, which the authors themselves identify as the likely reason Cartridges wins at extreme compaction ratios. The abstract's framing ('some of which admit efficient closed-form solutions') is accurate but slightly oversells the novelty relative to prior top-k selection heuristics; the genuinely new machinery is β and Cv fitting on top of subset selection.

Several evaluation protocols involve post-hoc subset construction: LongBench v2 is evaluated on a 47-context subset selected as 'correct with full context, incorrect without' (necessarily inducing selection effects), and Cartridges is only run on 20 of 50 QuALITY contexts. These are disclosed, but they weaken the strength of cross-method comparisons on those benchmarks, and LongHealth uses only 4 contexts.

Evaluation is limited to models up to 12B parameters and contexts of ~5–8k tokens for the primary benchmark (QuALITY); claims of scaling to larger MoE models are extrapolated (Section 4.4) rather than measured. The LongHealth evaluation required a different model variant and reduced context lengths relative to the original benchmark setup due to base-model context brittleness.

The nonuniform head-budget component, which the ablation identifies as the most important, relies on an approximate separability assumption across heads and is precomputed once per model; the paper does not test the failure modes of this assumption on out-of-distribution contexts beyond noting rankings are stable across two datasets.

No code release is stated anywhere in the manuscript, which limits reproducibility despite the detailed implementation appendices (solver choices, NNLS details, chunking variants); a method with this many implementation subtleties (reservoir sampling of queries, β stability constraints, KV- vs text-based chunking) benefits strongly from an artifact.

The per-token bias mechanism requires attention kernel support and modifies the cache representation (logical length T with physical size t); while the authors argue this is standard-supported, the systems-integration cost of the logical-length decoupling is not fully demonstrated in a serving context.

strengths: The core insight is elegant and well-executed: decomposing attention over concatenated blocks into a mixture weighted by unnormalized attention mass (Appendix A.2) cleanly motivates matching both attention outputs and attention mass, and the per-token bias β is shown to be necessary (not just convenient) for mass matching with t < T. This is a genuine conceptual contribution over prior eviction methods that only drop or merge tokens.

Avoiding gradient descent at compaction time via closed-form routines (NNLS for β, least squares for Cv, greedy OMP for key selection) is a well-designed algorithmic contribution that yields a family of methods tracing a speed–quality frontier (Figure 1), bridging the gap between fast heuristics (H2O, KVzip, summarization) and expensive optimization (Cartridges) at 2 orders of magnitude less compute.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough: 3 model families (including a sliding-window model), 4+ benchmarks (QuALITY, LongHealth, QASPER, LongBench v2, RULER, plus an AIME online-compaction proof of concept), comparisons against strong baselines including the prior SOTA (KVzip, Cartridges), and extensive ablations (Figure 5) showing every component (biases, learned values, head budgets, on-policy queries) contributes.

The nonuniform head-budget analysis (sensitivity curves that are largely input-invariant, precomputed per-model allocation) is a reusable insight that also illuminates why hybrid sliding-window architectures work, and is validated across models and datasets.

Honest and specific limitations discussion: the authors acknowledge Cartridges wins at 100× compaction on some benchmarks and attribute it to the restricted search space; the LongBench v2 subset-selection protocol is transparently described; the Online compaction result is presented as a proof of concept with tuning caveats.

Reproducibility support is strong: detailed algorithmic appendices (OMP variants, NNLS solver, numerical stability, chunking variants, self-study prompts, exact baseline configurations in Table 6), compute breakdowns (Table 3), and clear evaluation protocols.
weaknesses: Some central evaluations are small in scale: LongHealth uses only 4 contexts (400 questions), Cartridges is evaluated on only a 20-context Qwen-only subset of QuALITY, and LongBench v2 is restricted to a 47-context subset selected on a separate run with temperature-sampled decoding — this limits statistical power and introduces some risk of selection/bias effects, though the authors are transparent about each choice.

The abstract's 'achieving up to 50× compaction in seconds' is somewhat optimistic: the strongest variant (AM-OMP with self-study) takes several minutes per context (139s self-study + 565s OMP in Table 3), and 'seconds' applies only to the fastest variant; the paper itself concedes unoptimized OMP + self-study variants 'still required several minutes.'

The method is a collection of empirically motivated heuristics (RMS aggregation, OMP with periodic refit, greedy head-budget swaps, chunking choices) without theoretical guarantees on attention-output approximation error or on when reference-query distributions suffice; distribution shift from reference to actual future queries is mitigated (on-policy queries) but not fundamentally resolved.
No explicit statement of code release, which, given the many implementation details that affect results (NNLS warm-starts, β clamping bounds, chunking variants), would matter for community uptake.

Accuracy results in the main figures lack error bars or significance testing (only LongHealth context-level SEM appears in Figure 3), so gains of a few points over KVzip at some ratios are hard to assess.
The paper only evaluates models up to 12B parameters and a single MLA caveat is noted (G.2); scaling claims to larger MoE models remain extrapolation.
